questions.q: All of the following are risk factors for diabetic retinopathy per p160 EXCEPT:
opts: High myopia of more than 6 dioptres
Poor glycemic control with a high HbA1c
Pregnancy, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and diabetic nephropathy
questions.exp: Risk factors: duration of diabetes, high HbA1c, pregnancy, hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and diabetic nephropathy. (Book p160)

questions.q: Match the type of diabetes with the time of first screening for retinopathy per p160 — 1) Type 1 diabetes 2) Type 2 diabetes … A) As soon as possible after diagnosis B) After 5 years
questions.exp: Time of screening: type 1 diabetes - after 5 years; type 2 diabetes - as soon as possible. (Book p160)

questions.q: Screening for retinopathy in type 1 diabetes mellitus should begin after:
questions.exp: Time of screening: type 1 DM after 5 years; type 2 DM as soon as possible. (Book p160)

questions.q: A pregnant woman with long standing diabetes is reviewed in the retina clinic. Per p160, pregnancy is listed as:
opts: An indication to stop all laser treatment
A risk factor that accelerates diabetic retinopathy
questions.exp: Risk factors for diabetic retinopathy: duration of diabetes, high HbA1c, pregnancy, hypertension/hyperlipidemia and diabetic nephropathy. (Book p160)

questions.q: True/false per p160: duration of diabetes is itself a risk factor for diabetic retinopathy.
opts: False — retinopathy is unrelated to disease duration
questions.exp: Risk factors: duration of diabetes is a risk (along with HbA1c, pregnancy, hypertension/hyperlipidemia and diabetic nephropathy). (Book p160)

questions.q: Match the pathogenetic change in diabetic retinopathy with its category per p160 — 1) Protein kinase C activation 2) Increased sorbitol 3) Loss of pericytes of capillaries 4) Secretion of VEGF … A) Biochemical change B) Anatomical vascular lesion
questions.exp: Biochemical changes: protein kinase C activation, increased sorbitol, reactive oxygen intermediates and advanced glycation end products. Anatomical vascular lesions: loss of pericytes of capillaries (earliest change), leakage from capillaries, neovascularization of retina (hallmark) from secretion of VEGF. (Book p160)

questions.q: The earliest anatomical change in diabetic retinopathy per p160 is:
questions.exp: Anatomical vascular lesions: loss of pericytes of capillaries is the earliest change. (Book p160)

questions.q: The hallmark of diabetic retinopathy per p160 is:
opts: Neovascularization of the retina, driven by secretion of VEGF
questions.exp: Neovascularization of the retina is the hallmark of diabetic retinopathy, occurring with secretion of VEGF. (Book p160)

questions.q: All of the following are biochemical changes in diabetic retinopathy per p160 EXCEPT:
opts: Accumulation of advanced glycation end products
questions.exp: Biochemical changes: protein kinase C activation, increased sorbitol, reactive oxygen intermediates and advanced glycation end products. Loss of pericytes is an anatomical vascular lesion. (Book p160)

questions.q: Match the lesion of diabetic retinopathy with its appearance per p161 — 1) Microaneurysms 2) Exudates 3) Cotton wool spots 4) Neovascularization … A) Large yellowish deposits with regular smooth edges B) Yellowish irregular deposits C) Tortuous tuft of vessel D) Tiny red dots
questions.exp: Microaneurysms: O/E tiny red dots, FFA tiny hyperfluorescent dots. Exudates: O/E yellowish irregular deposits, FFA hypofluorescent. Cotton wool spots: O/E large yellowish deposits with regular smooth edges, FFA hypofluorescent. Neovascularization: O/E tortuous tuft of vessel, FFA hyperfluorescent. (Book p161)

questions.q: Retinal hemorrhages in diabetic retinopathy per p161 are described as:
opts: Flame shaped in the superficial nerve fibre layer and dot and blot in the deeper layers
questions.exp: Hemorrhage: flame shaped in the superficial nerve fibre layer; dot and blot hemorrhages in the deeper (outer plexiform/inner nuclear) layers. (Book p161)

questions.q: Hard exudates in diabetic retinopathy per p161 are:
opts: Collections of neuronal debris in the nerve fibre layer
Lipid deposits in the outer plexiform layer
questions.exp: Exudates: lipid deposits in the outer plexiform layer. (Book p161)

questions.q: Cotton wool spots (soft exudates) per p161 are:
opts: Collections of neuronal debris in the nerve fibre layer
Lipid deposits in the outer plexiform layer
questions.exp: Cotton wool spots (soft exudates): collections of neuronal debris in the nerve fibre layer. (Book p161)

questions.q: Venous tortuosity with beading and looping in diabetic retinopathy per p161 is due to:
opts: Vasculitic damage to the vein wall
questions.exp: Venous tortuosity: due to hypoxia, with beading and looping. (Book p161)

questions.q: Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) per p161 are:
opts: Dilated capillaries in the foveal avascular zone
New vessels growing through the internal limiting membrane
Shunt vessels bypassing the capillary bed and a precursor of proliferative disease
Collaterals at the optic disc after a vein occlusion
questions.exp: IRMA: intraretinal microvascular abnormalities - shunt vessels bypassing the capillary bed, a precursor to PDR. (Book p161)

questions.q: Match the type of retinal neovascularization with its definition per p161 — 1) NVD 2) NVE … A) New vessels elsewhere in the retina B) New vessels at the disc or within one disc diameter of it
questions.exp: PDR: NVD = new vessels at the disc or within 1 disc diameter of it; NVE = new vessels elsewhere. (Book p161)

questions.q: All of the following are features of non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy per p161 EXCEPT:
opts: Microaneurysms and dot and blot hemorrhages
Cotton wool spots and hard exudates
Venous beading and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities
questions.exp: NPDR lesions: microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots, venous tortuosity/beading/looping and IRMA. Neovascularization (NVD/NVE) defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy. (Book p161)

questions.q: Match the stage of NPDR with the follow up interval per p162 — 1) Mild 2) Moderate 3) Severe 4) Very severe … A) 4 months B) 9-12 months C) 2 months D) 6 months
questions.exp: NPDR follow up: mild 9-12 months, moderate 6 months, severe 4 months, very severe 2 months. (Book p162)

questions.q: Fill up per p162: the first general measure in the treatment of diabetic retinopathy is ____ control:
questions.exp: Treatment of diabetic retinopathy: glycemic control, then stage-wise follow up, pan retinal photocoagulation or anti-VEGF drugs. (Book p162)

questions.q: The 4-2-1 rule of NPDR per p162 refers to:
opts: 4 disc areas of new vessels, 2 disc areas of fibrosis, 1 disc area of detachment
Microaneurysms in 4 quadrants, exudates in 2 quadrants, cotton wool spots in 1 quadrant
Follow up at 4 months, laser in 2 sittings, review at 1 month
Hemorrhage in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 quadrants, IRMA in 1 quadrant
questions.exp: 4-2-1 rule of NPDR: 4 quadrants of hemorrhage, 2 quadrants of venous beading, 1 quadrant of IRMA. (Book p162)

questions.q: Applying the 4-2-1 rule per p162: any one feature means severe NPDR and any two mean:
questions.exp: Any 1 of the 4-2-1 features = severe NPDR; any 2 = very severe NPDR. (Book p162)

questions.q: Treatment of choice for proliferative diabetic retinopathy per p162 is:
opts: Focal laser photocoagulation of leaking microaneurysms
Pan retinal photocoagulation with an argon green laser in multiple sittings
Pars plana vitrectomy in every case
questions.exp: PDR treatment: pan retinal photocoagulation is the TOC, using an argon green laser in multiple sittings; anti-VEGF drugs are the other option. (Book p162)

questions.q: Side effect of pan retinal photocoagulation per p162 is:
opts: Raised intraocular pressure in every patient
questions.exp: Pan retinal photocoagulation: argon green laser, multiple sittings; side effect - visual field defects. (Book p162)

questions.q: Match the indication for treating proliferative diabetic retinopathy per p162 — 1) NVD 2) NVE … A) New vessels more than half a disc area elsewhere with vitreous hemorrhage B) New vessels more than one third of the disc area, or NVD with vitreous hemorrhage
questions.exp: Indication for treatment: NVD >1/3 disc area, NVD with vitreous hemorrhage, or NVE >1/2 disc area with vitreous hemorrhage. (Book p162)

questions.q: All of the following anti-VEGF drugs are listed for diabetic retinopathy on p162 EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Anti-VEGF drugs listed: ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept and brolucizumab. Verteporfin is a photosensitising drug used in photodynamic therapy. (Book p162)

questions.q: Diabetic macular edema per p162 is due to leakage from capillaries and is:
opts: The most common cause of neovascular glaucoma
The most common cause of loss of vision in non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy
A feature only of proliferative disease
Always self limiting within three months
questions.exp: Diabetic macular edema: d/t leakage from capillaries; m/c cause of loss of vision in NPDR (diabetic retinopathy). (Book p162)

questions.q: Treatment of choice for diabetic macular edema per p162 is:
questions.exp: Rx of diabetic macular edema: 1. focal laser photocoagulation is the TOC; 2. intravitreal triamcinolone; 3. anti-VEGF drugs. (Book p162)

questions.q: A pseudophakic patient with ischemic maculopathy and significant cardiovascular disease needs treatment for diabetic macular edema. Per p162 the preferred option is:
questions.exp: Indications for intravitreal triamcinolone: ischemic maculopathy, pseudophakic patient and coexisting cardiovascular disease. (Book p162)

questions.q: Anti-VEGF therapy in diabetic macular edema per p162 is indicated for:
opts: Exudates more than two disc diameters from the fovea
Vitreous hemorrhage with a clear macula
questions.exp: Anti-VEGF drugs: indication is centre involving edema (central foveal thickness measured within 300 micrometres of the fovea). (Book p162)

questions.q: Clinically significant macular edema (CSME) per p162 includes retinal thickening or exudates within:
opts: 1500 micrometres of the centre of the macula only
500 micrometres of the centre of the macula, or a lesion over one disc diameter in size within one disc diameter (1500 micrometres) of it
2 disc diameters of the fovea regardless of size
questions.exp: CSME: retinal thickening within 500 micrometres of the centre of the macula; exudates within 500 micrometres of the centre of the macula (with retinal thickening anywhere); or retinal thickening/exudates larger than 1 DD within 1 DD (1500 micrometres) of the centre of the macula. (Book p162)

questions.q: Match the cause of vitreous hemorrhage with the patient group per p163 — 1) Adults 2) Young adults 3) Young patients … A) Blunt trauma B) Eale's disease C) Diabetic retinopathy
questions.exp: Causes of vitreous hemorrhage: in adults - diabetic retinopathy; in young adults - blunt trauma; in the young - Eale's disease. (Book p163)

questions.q: Management of vitreous hemorrhage in diabetic retinopathy per p163:
opts: Large hemorrhage is observed and only small hemorrhage is operated
All patients need immediate pars plana vitrectomy
All patients are treated with intravitreal antibiotics
Small hemorrhage is observed; large or recurrent hemorrhage needs endophotocoagulation or pars plana vitrectomy
questions.exp: Vitreous hemorrhage Rx: small - observe; large/recurrent - endophotocoagulation or pars plana vitrectomy. (Book p163)

questions.q: Rubeosis iridis, a complication of diabetic retinopathy per p163, is:
opts: Neovascularisation of the iris driven by the oxygen demand of the posterior segment
Pigment dispersion from the iris pigment epithelium
An inflammatory nodule on the iris
questions.exp: Rubeosis iridis: neovascularisation of the iris, d/t the oxygen demand of the posterior segment. (Book p163)

questions.q: All of the following are listed complications of diabetic retinopathy on p162-163 EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Complications of diabetic retinopathy: 1. diabetic macular edema; 2. vitreous hemorrhage; 3. retinal detachment; 4. rubeosis iridis (neovascularisation of the iris). (Book p163)
